title: One Goddess, nine forms
hookLine: nine nights, nine forms, and a battlefield where the Goddess says there's no one else
carry: ekam sat: one truth, many names
last: THE LORD OF OBSTACLES HUMBLES PRIDE.

cards: Near the shrine in a North Indian home during Navaratri, you may find a small calendar taped up: one name for each night, all the way to nine. Some families wear a different color each day to match.
It looks like nine goddesses. Ask the grandmother who keeps the calendar, and she'll likely tell you: it's one Goddess, nine ways.

teach.b: The nine forms are the Navadurga, nine Durgas, and in the common list they move through a life: Shailaputri, daughter of the mountain; Brahmacharini, the seeker who fasts in the forest to win Shiva; Chandraghanta and Kushmanda; Skandamata, the mother; Katyayani, the warrior; Kalaratri, the dark night who destroys fear; Mahagauri, radiant and calm; and Siddhidatri, giver of every attainment.

teach.h: DAUGHTER, SEEKER, MOTHER, WARRIOR, DARK NIGHT, PEACE.
teach.b: Devotees honor one each night, and many fast. So are they nine goddesses? The Devi Mahatmya, the scripture many read aloud through Navaratri, answers with a story.
The demon king Shumbha has watched a whole army of goddesses fight beside Durga. Furious, he taunts her: you're proud, but you only win by leaning on other women's strength.
And the Goddess answers: I am alone here in the world.

teach.h: WHO ELSE IS THERE BESIDES ME?
teach.b: Who else is there besides me? These are my own powers, coming back into me.
And every goddess on the field disappears into her body, until she stands alone and faces him herself.

That's one of Hinduism's oldest and biggest teachings, and the answer to anyone who asks if Hindus have nine goddesses, or a thousand gods. The Rig Veda says it in four words: ekam sat vipra bahudha vadanti.

teach.h: EKAM SAT: ONE TRUTH, MANY NAMES.
teach.b: Truth is one; the wise call it by many names. Many forms, one reality.
And on the eighth or ninth day, many families invite young girls home, wash their feet, feed them and honor them as the Goddess: one more form she takes.

how: Many Hindus honor one of the nine forms of Durga, the Navadurga, on each night of Navaratri, with that form's prayers and offerings; some fast all nine days, some wear a set color each day, and many end by honoring young girls as the Goddess on the eighth or ninth day.

o: one Goddess honored in nine forms over nine nights
nine separate goddesses, each with her own festival

p: the dark night, who destroys fear

the Rig Veda says truth is one, and the wise call it by many names
ekam sat vipra bahudha vadanti: many forms, one reality.
in the Devi Mahatmya, the goddesses leave Durga to fight alone
they go back into her: they were her own powers all along.

games.q: Shumbha sneers: you only win with other goddesses' help. you're the Goddess. what do you say?
o: 'there's no one else. they're my own powers, coming home.'
games.why: in the Devi Mahatmya she draws every goddess back into herself and stands alone: many forms, one Goddess.

practice: Many families honor one form of the Goddess each night. Pick the one that fits your week: the seeker who doesn't give up, the mother, the warrior, or the dark night who destroys fear.
Say her name softly on a few breaths out, then let it rest into one word: Ma, mother. If you don't pray, name the strength you need, then notice it's the same strength under every name.

wordCard.voice: Navaratri. Nine nights, nine forms, the Navadurga, and one Goddess under every name.

orig.note: Sanskrit nava (nine) + durgā (the one hard to approach): the nine forms of the Goddess.

carryVoice: Your line: ekam sat, one truth, many names. Durga said it on the battlefield: who else is there besides me? Day six hundred seventy-nine, done.
